title: Invoicing and billing
brief: Small businesses create invoices, email them to customers and take card payments online. On the last working day of the month everyone sends and chases invoices at once. Nobody may get the same invoice email twice, and no invoice may vanish.

clarify.q: Can an invoice be edited after it is sent?
clarify.a: Only by issuing a new version. Every version is kept, so every write is a durable new record.

clarify.q: Do emails have to arrive instantly?
clarify.a: Provider acceptance within 120 seconds is fine. Use a stable provider key and reconcile unknown outcomes after a crash. Without provider support, one external email delivery cannot be guaranteed.
A payment provider. It is the slow part: about half a second typically, and it limits how fast you may call it.

notes: An invoice page is about 4 KB; a PDF copy is made later.
Month-end brings about 3 times the normal peak.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.label: Card payments per second at peak

hints: Emails do not need to be sent while the customer waits. What could take a message and let someone else deliver it?
A queue plus a worker pool turns the email burst into a steady trickle. The email provider limits how fast it accepts mail, so a queue also protects it.
Use a load balancer, 4 servers over 2 zones, a cache in front of the database, a queue and workers for email, and an idempotency store so a payment or an email is never done twice.

editorial.summary: The web part is plain: balance, a few servers, a cache for the invoice pages people reopen all day, and one database. The part that earns the points is the email path. Month-end sends thousands of mails in minutes, and the queue redelivers some of them. A queue absorbs the burst, workers send at a safe pace, and an idempotency store makes a second delivery of the same email do nothing.

designs.name: Cache, queue and idempotency keys
designs.why: Servers answer pages from a cache, the database only sees saves, and email leaves through a queue so it never slows a page. A small key table remembers which payments and emails were already done.

tradeoffs: The cache makes invoice pages fast and cheap, but a page can be up to 5 minutes behind the last edit. Invoices rarely change, so that is fine here.
The queue means "sent" really means "accepted"; delivery follows seconds later. In return the email provider never sees a burst.
Idempotency keys cost a small table and one lookup per payment, and they remove the worst bug in billing: charging or emailing twice.
Two zones double the database cost. For an invoicing tool that is worth it, because losing the primary would otherwise stop all billing for an hour.
editorial.realWorld: Invoicing tools often send tens of millions of emails a month, and their busiest hour is the last day of the month, roughly 3 to 5 times a normal hour (approx.).

correctness.prompt: A worker sends a message, then crashes before recording success. What key and delivery states would you store so a retry does not send it twice?
correctness.discussion: Give each logical message a stable key, scoped to its recipient and channel, and enforce a unique constraint on that key. Save the request and an outbox entry in one transaction, then track pending, sending and delivered states. A queue alone does not prevent duplicates. If the provider accepts the send but the worker crashes, retry with the same provider idempotency key or query its status. Without provider support, exactly-once external delivery cannot be guaranteed: discuss whether a possible duplicate or a possible missed message is acceptable.

fields.label: The provider accepts the operation, then the worker crashes before saving success. What state is durable?
options: Unknown outcome, with the original logical operation key
Failed, so the retry gets a new key
fields.explanation: Missing local success does not prove the provider rejected the operation.

fields.label: The queue redelivers that operation. What can establish one external effect?
options: Check a local cache, then send without a provider key
Reuse the provider idempotency key or reconcile its recorded outcome
fields.explanation: A local lookup and a remote side effect are not atomic. Without endpoint support, one external effect cannot be guaranteed; report uncertainty and choose an explicit recovery policy.
